extracted.intended_audience: paleontologists, historians/philosophers of science, and graduate students in paleobiology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for constructing, testing, and interpreting evolutionary/paleontological models and claims (e.g., nomothetic vs idiographic approaches, simulation design, evidentiary standards, and what would constitute disciplinary autonomy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomothetic approach / abstraction from taxa peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract the common elements hidden beneath the bewildering peculiarities of individual taxa by constructing models that make no reference to the peculiarities of individual taxa; treat species as biologically undifferentiated particles where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nomothetic strategy asks that one assume nothing about individual taxa beyond origination and extinction points, so predictions about diversity can be made from general processes (e.g., immigration vs extinction curves). Use this approach when searching for laws of nature that operate independent of time, space, and taxonomic group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative model assumptions (minimal biological detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate models that only specify the branching/appearance/disappearance format and avoid making assumptions about specific evolutionary mechanisms, genetic or morphological change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MBL simulations specified at each time step: (1) go extinct, (2) produce another lineage and persist, or (3) persist without producing another lineage. Such conservative assumptions allow testing whether high-level patterns can arise without invoking detailed organismal differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null/random-model testing before inferring directed causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept directional or adaptive explanations for observed 'order' if the same patterns can be generated by random processes; an orderly pattern supplies no proof for uni-directional selection if it can be produced by random models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stochastic simulations and null models to see whether observed features (trends, correlations, morphological coherence) require adaptive explanations or can be artifacts of random origination/extinction. Treat such null-model results as a warning against over-interpreting patterns as evidence of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic parameterization and sensitivity testing (e.g., clade size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulations and models must use empirically realistic parameter values (for example, typical standing clade sizes) because unrealistic values (e.g., very small average clade size) can produce exaggerated stochastic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanley et al.'s critique showed MBL's small average clade sizes (~4 lineages) produced high variability not seen in larger, realistic clades. Test sensitivity of results to parameter changes (clade size, branching/extinction probabilities) to ensure patterns are robust and not artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive, quantitative testability
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable model should make quantitative predictions about what we ought to see in the fossil record (e.g., properties of clades across time) so its claims are testable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to make numerical/graphical predictions distinguishes a fruitful approach; present quantitative predictions and compare them to empirical data. Graphical presentation can influence acceptance but must be supported by sound predictions and tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, generality, and explanatory reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor simple models with relatively few, well-understood parameters that are general and deeply intuitive on a biological level; simplicity aids understanding and broad applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gould favored simple functional forms (e.g., power functions) not because they are always most accurate but because their simplicity and generality make them useful explanatory tools. Balance simplicity with empirical adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real phenomena from by-products or artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a proposed evolutionary phenomenon (e.g., variability of clade diversity, stasis) is a direct consequence of an underlying process rather than a by-product of other population genetic processes or sampling/artifact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the phenomenon would occur under the proposed mechanism even when controlling for alternative explanations (e.g., population genetic processes, sampling biases, clade size). If an existing theory already predicts the phenomenon (e.g., morphological trends predicted by population genetics), justify why a new explanation is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of analysis (Markovian vs non‑Markovian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a level of analysis suited to the phenomenon: genetic-level processes may be Markovian (depend only on current state), whereas higher-level processes (e.g., extinction dynamics) may require non‑Markovian analyses because history might be irrelevant or differently relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Van Valen's Law (constant extinction rate with taxon age) suggests at the clade/extinction level history may be irrelevant; recognize when higher-level processes behave differently from genic selection and adapt analytic frameworks accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simulations to evaluate whether organismal differences are required
rubrics_metrics.description: If random (organism‑indifferent) models reproduce observed patterns, then observed differences between clades do not necessarily demand explanations invoking organismal peculiarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MBL simulations showed that a range of clade shapes and patterns could arise without intrinsic biological differences. Use simulations as a methodological check before attributing patterns to inherent differences among taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standards for claiming disciplinary autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim a new disciplinary autonomy one must (1) identify a set of related problems whose solution is in sufficiently high demand, and (2) have a privileged perspective uniquely well suited to solve those problems; additionally continuity (practice differences should track differences in fitness) matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the research program both supplies solutions to problems that are sought by the community and possesses distinctive tools/insights unavailable elsewhere. The MBL work had the privileged perspective (fossil record insight) but arguably failed on demand for certain problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare proposed explanations against existing well‑developed theories
rubrics_metrics.description: When an existing framework (e.g., population genetics) already offers detailed mathematical explanations for a phenomenon (e.g., morphological trends), a new model must either make novel testable predictions or explain phenomena that the existing theory cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the problem the new model addresses is of sufficient demand (not already solved) and whether the new model offers superior explanatory power or new predictions; otherwise its scholarly impact will be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and communication matter but don't substitute for validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The form in which results are presented (graphical/visual choices) can affect how persuasive they are to practitioners, but persuasive graphics do not replace methodological correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that effective visualization can aid acceptance; nevertheless ensure the underlying model, assumptions, and tests are robust and transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for claiming broad laws (independence from time/space/taxon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a law operates 'independent of time, space, and taxonomic group' require demonstration that the pattern is insensitive to peculiarities of taxa, temporal contexts, and spatial contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proposed law relies on the freedom from phenotypic detail, show through modeling and empirical comparison that it holds across diverse taxa, times, and places; otherwise the claim to universality is unwarranted.
